summary: Describes an unencrypted form of the Kerberos 5 KRB-CRED message, which transfers Kerberos credentials between applications. When a secure transport already protects the exchange, leaving out the extra encryption can be useful.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6448 formally describes an unencrypted form of the Kerberos KRB-CRED message for transferring credentials. It must be carried only by a transport that provides confidentiality, integrity, mutual authentication, and established identities.

questions: when to use unencrypted kerberos credentials
what is the unencrypted krb-cred form
what does kerberos etype 0 mean here
subtitle: A defined way to transfer Kerberos credentials without message-level encryption over a protected transport.

tldr.problem: Applications may need to transfer Kerberos credentials without already sharing Kerberos keys, while another transport protects the exchange.
tldr.mechanism: The KRB-CRED message uses encryption type 0 as a message-specific signal and carries a cleartext copy of the credential part.
tldr.outcome: The form is allowed only over a transport that provides confidentiality, integrity, mutual authentication, and known identities.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 6448's status as Proposed Standard. The RFC specifies an unencrypted KRB-CRED form for use only with a suitably protected transport.

sections.title: When an Unencrypted KRB-CRED Is Useful
sections.content:
KRB-CRED transfers Kerberos credentials between applications. Some applications need to transfer credentials without having an established relationship based on Kerberos keys.

If the transport already provides confidentiality and integrity, the RFC allows the unencrypted form of KRB-CRED to carry the credentials. The document formalizes a form that some existing implementations had used.
sections.plainLanguage: The message can omit its own encryption when another secure connection protects it. The transport must provide the protection the message itself lacks.

sections.title: The Unencrypted Message Form
sections.content:
The message contains an EncryptedData structure whose encryption type must be 0. The optional key version number should not be present, and a recipient must ignore it if it is present.

The ciphertext field contains a cleartext copy of EncKrbCredPart. In this KRB-CRED context, type 0 signals that the message is not encrypted; it is not an encryption system.
sections.plainLanguage: The message uses the value 0 to say that its credential part is cleartext. The value is a signal for this message format, not an encryption method.

sections.title: Required Protection from the Transport
sections.content:
KRB-CRED contains sensitive information such as session keys, principal names, and validity periods. An attacker who obtains the credential information and ticket could impersonate the named client; changing the message could also cause the recipient to use unintended credentials.

The unencrypted form must be used only over a transport where sender and recipient identities are known to each other and that provides confidentiality, integrity, and mutual authentication. The RFC gives mutually authenticated TLS as one example.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who steals or changes these credentials may cause serious harm. Use the unencrypted form only when the surrounding connection protects the message and verifies both parties.
